name: Dostoevsky
era: 1821 to 1881, and the conscience of the novel ever since
line: Do not lie to yourself, love the person in front of you, and answer for everyone.

quote.by: Prince Myshkin, as Ippolit reports it
quote.source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Idiot, 1869, Part 3, chapter 5

quotes.text: Above all, do not lie to yourself.
Love all of God’s creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand.
quotes.source: The Brothers Karamazov, 1880, Book 6, chapter 3; wording varies by translation

quotes.text: Each of us is guilty before everyone, for everyone and for everything.
quotes.source: The Brothers Karamazov, 1880, Book 6, chapter 2; wording varies by translation

quotes.text: To go wrong in one’s own way is better than to go right in someone else’s.
quotes.source: Crime and Punishment, 1866, Part 3, chapter 1, trans. Constance Garnett

quotes.text: Man is a mystery. It must be solved, and if you spend your whole life solving it, do not say you have wasted your time.
quotes.source: Letter to his brother Mikhail, 16 August 1839

quotes.text: The soul is healed by being with children.
quotes.source: The Idiot, 1869, Part 1, chapter 6; wording varies by translation

words.usage: The inner person, the seat of conscience and feeling. Russians use it every day: to talk po dushe is to talk heart to heart.
A spiritual ache with no clear object. Nabokov said no English word renders all its shades.
A person who seems mad or simple and speaks truth to power. Myshkin is the great holy fool of the novel.
A monk to whom people come for counsel. Zosima is modelled partly on the elders of Optina Pustyn.
The native ground. Dostoevsky wanted the educated to return to the soil of the people and their faith.
The movement he shaped with his brother in their journal Vremya in the 1860s.
Feelings pushed past their truth into display and torment. Book 4 of The Brothers Karamazov is named for it.
Not weakness but a terrible strength, says Zosima: loving humility is the strongest force of all.
A constant subject. His characters seek it, flee it and are changed by it; the Onda never asks for it.
Myshkin calls compassion the chief and perhaps the only law of human existence.
What finally undoes Raskolnikov: not the police but his own conscience.
The cellar of the mind where spite and wounded pride live. Notes from Underground gave it its name.
A second self that acts out what the first denies. The title of his second novel, 1846.
A word of the Slavophile Khomyakov for a free communion of persons, close to Zosima’s vision.
A small oil lamp of coloured glass kept burning before an icon. It glows through his rooms and novels.
A holy image painted to be prayed with, not merely looked at.
The corner of a room where the icons hang. Krasny once meant beautiful before it meant red.
The midsummer weeks in Petersburg when the sky never darkens. The title of his tale of a dreamer.
The Siberian hard labour he served in Omsk from 1850 to 1854.
The stockade where convicts lived. The House of the Dead describes it.
The heated urn of Russian life. He drank his tea so strong it was nearly black.
His ruin in Wiesbaden and Baden-Baden, and the working title of The Gambler.
The Karamazov blend of sensual force, wildness and thirst for life. The word is used inside the novel.
Possessing ideas. The title of his 1872 novel of conspirators.
The lonely young man of White Nights who lives in fantasies rather than days.
Ivan Karamazov’s poem of the old cardinal who arrests Christ for having made people free.
Ivan’s conclusion if there is no God and no immortality. Smerdyakov acts on it.
Zosima’s answer to doubt: love your neighbours actively and tirelessly, and faith follows.
Bakhtin’s word for his novels: many full voices, none silenced by the author’s.
Also the root of the old Russian farewell, prosti, which means both forgive me and goodbye.
Sonya reads Raskolnikov the raising of Lazarus. The Easter greeting is Khristos voskrese, Christ is risen.

practices.name: Do not lie to yourself
practices.instructions: Before you look at your phone, sit for five minutes and ask one plain question: what am I pretending not to know? It may be about your work, a friendship, your health or your own motives. Do not solve it. Just say it to yourself in one honest sentence, quietly or on paper, and carry that sentence into the day.
practices.why: Zosima’s first counsel is not to lie to yourself, because every other lie grows from that one. Dostoevsky’s characters fall when they deceive themselves and begin to heal when they stop.
variations: Write the sentence on a slip of paper and keep it in your pocket.
Ask it about one person you find difficult.
Ask it about something you are proud of.

practices.name: Light the lamp
practices.instructions: Light a candle or a small lamp in one corner of your room, before a picture, an icon or simply a window. Sit facing it for three minutes. Let your breathing slow. Think of one person you will meet today and hold them in the light for a moment, wishing them well. Then put the flame out carefully and begin.
practices.why: Russian homes kept a lampada burning before the icons in the beautiful corner. His rooms had one, and its small red glow runs through his novels as a sign of a faith that keeps watch in the dark.
variations: Use a lamp with coloured glass, red or green, as Russians did.
Hold someone you are at odds with in the light.
Keep the lamp lit while you eat breakfast.

practices.name: The first person you meet
practices.instructions: Decide now that the first person you speak to today will receive your full attention and a real kindness, whoever they are: a child, a partner, a neighbour, the bus driver. Look at their face. Ask one question and listen to the answer. Do one small thing for them that you did not have to do. Notice how it changes your morning.
practices.why: Active love, says Zosima, is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. It begins not with humanity but with the person who happens to be in front of you.
variations: Make it the person you usually overlook.
Remember their name and use it.
Do it again with the second person.

practices.name: A page of the Gospel he carried
practices.instructions: Read one short passage slowly, the way he read the New Testament he carried through four years of prison. John 11, the raising of Lazarus, is the one Sonya reads to Raskolnikov. Or read the Sermon on the Mount, or any page of wisdom you love. Read it twice. Stop at the line that catches you and stay with it.
practices.why: The wives of the Decembrists gave him a New Testament on his way to Siberia. It was the only book allowed in the camp, and he kept it all his life. Slow reading of a few lines can do what a hundred pages cannot.
variations: Read the passage aloud.
Copy the line that caught you by hand.
Read a page of The Brothers Karamazov, Book 6, instead.

practices.name: Strong tea and three tasks
practices.instructions: Make a pot of tea stronger than usual, the way he drank it. While it steeps, write down only three things you must do today, the three that truly matter, in order. Leave everything else off the list. Drink the tea slowly and look at the three lines. Begin the first one before you do anything else.
practices.why: He worked under crushing deadlines, debts and illness, and still finished the greatest novels of his century, often by deciding what must be written tonight and doing only that.
variations: Use a glass in a holder, as Russians drink tea.
Sweeten it with a spoon of jam instead of sugar.
Write the three tasks the night before.

practices.name: Kiss the earth
practices.instructions: Go outside, to a garden, a park, a patch of grass or even a potted plant. Crouch down and touch the earth with both hands. Feel its cold or warmth. Think of all the life it carries and everything that has lived and died on it. Say thank you, silently or aloud. Wash your hands only afterwards.
practices.why: Alyosha, after Zosima’s death, falls to the earth and kisses it, weeping, and rises a fighter for life. Love the earth, says Zosima, and every grain of sand in it.
variations: Walk barefoot on grass for a minute.
Plant one seed.
Pick up litter from a small patch of ground.

practices.name: One concrete kindness
practices.instructions: Do one practical, unglamorous good deed for someone who will probably not thank you: carry a neighbour’s shopping, buy a meal for someone who asks for money, call a lonely relative, clean a shared space nobody cleans. Keep it real and specific. Do not tell anyone about it afterwards.
practices.why: Ivan Karamazov loves humanity in general and cannot bear his neighbour. Dostoevsky’s answer is love that does something now, for someone, without an audience.
variations: Give something you would rather keep.
Choose a stranger.
Do it for someone who has wronged you.

practices.name: Find your underground
practices.instructions: Watch yourself for a moment of spite today: when you wanted to win more than to be right, refused help out of pride, or did something against your own interest just to make a point. When you catch it, stop and name it to yourself without excuses. Then ask what wounded pride sits underneath.
practices.why: The man from underground will act against his own good just to prove he is free. Dostoevsky saw that this spite lives in everyone, and that seeing it clearly is the first step out of the cellar.
variations: Write down the moment and what you felt.
Do the opposite of what spite wanted.
Notice spite in your online life.

practices.name: Walk Raskolnikov’s city
practices.instructions: Walk for half an hour through a part of your town you usually avoid: a market, a crowded square, a poor street. Walk slowly and look at faces, doorways, courtyards and windows. Notice who is tired, who is alone, who is laughing. Do not take photographs. Let the city speak to you as Petersburg spoke to him.
practices.why: His novels walk the Haymarket and its back streets among drunks, students, mothers and pawnbrokers. He believed every face hides a whole world and that the city reveals the soul to those who look.
variations: Sit on a bench for ten minutes and only watch.
Walk at dusk.
Buy something small from a street seller and talk with them.

practices.name: Listen without fixing
practices.instructions: Have one conversation today in which you only listen. Let the other person finish every thought. Do not offer advice, correct them or turn it to your own story. Ask one more question when they pause. If you disagree, let their view stand at full strength in your mind for a while before you answer.
practices.why: Bakhtin saw that Dostoevsky lets every character speak with a full voice, even those he disagreed with. Truth, in his novels, happens between people who truly hear one another.
variations: Listen to someone older than you about their life.
Listen to a view you dislike, in full.
Repeat back what you heard before answering.

practices.name: Ask forgiveness first
practices.instructions: Think of one person you are in a quiet quarrel with, even a small one. Without waiting to work out who was more wrong, ask their forgiveness for your part. Say it simply, in person, by message or by letter. Do not add a but. Then let it go, whatever they answer.
practices.why: Zosima’s brother asks forgiveness of the servants and the birds; Zosima himself asks it of the officer he was about to duel. In Dostoevsky the first to ask forgiveness is the freest person in the room.
variations: Ask forgiveness of someone who has died, in a letter you keep.
Ask forgiveness of a child.
Forgive someone who has not asked.

practices.name: Write like a stenographer
practices.instructions: Speak your thoughts on something that troubles you aloud for twenty minutes while writing them down as fast as you can, or record yourself and write it out. Do not stop to correct anything. Let the voices in you argue. Read it back only at the end, and underline the one sentence that surprised you.
practices.why: From The Gambler on he dictated his novels to Anna, who took them down in shorthand. Speaking let the voices of his characters run free before he shaped them.
variations: Let two sides of yourself argue on the page.
Dictate a letter to someone you love.
Write by hand only, no screens.

practices.name: The day’s honest account
practices.instructions: Before bed, write a short, honest account of your day in your journal. Where did you lie to yourself? Where did you love actively, and where did you only dream of loving? Whom did you judge? Write plainly, without punishing yourself. End with one thing you are grateful for.
practices.why: Dostoevsky kept notebooks full of arguments with himself. Honesty without self-torment is the point: Zosima warns against the laceration of feelings pushed into display.
variations: Use one of the Onda’s journal prompts.
Write it as a letter to Zosima.
Write only three lines, but true ones.

practices.name: Responsible for all
practices.instructions: Think back over the day and pick one thing that went wrong around you, at work, at home or in the news. Instead of asking whose fault it was, ask what small part of it is yours to answer for, even indirectly. Decide on one thing you could do tomorrow about that part.
practices.why: Each of us is guilty before all for all, says Markel. Not as a burden of guilt but as an end to standing outside, which, says Zosima, turns the world into paradise.
variations: Think of a stranger affected by your choices.
Think of the people who made your clothes.
Do the thing tomorrow before noon.

practices.name: Read by lamplight
practices.instructions: Turn off the overhead lights and read for half an hour by a single lamp or candle. Read Dostoevsky if you can: White Nights for a gentle evening, a chapter of The Brothers Karamazov for a long one. Read slowly, and stop to listen to a character you dislike as carefully as one you love.
practices.why: His was a world of oil lamps and long winter evenings. Reading in a small pool of light slows the eye and lets a voice from the page come close.
variations: Read aloud to someone.
Read the Grand Inquisitor chapter in one sitting.
Read a page of his letters.

practices.name: The night writer
practices.instructions: Write for twenty minutes late in the evening, when the house is quiet. A letter, a page of a story, a confession, a memory. Have a glass of tea beside you. Write without planning and without looking at your phone. When you stop, put the pages away unread until tomorrow.
practices.why: He did his writing at night, from late evening until dawn, with strong tea, and slept into the morning. Night writing reaches places the busy day keeps closed.
variations: Write a memory from your childhood.
Write as one of his characters.
Write a letter you will not send.

practices.name: Hold someone in prayer
practices.instructions: Before sleep, name to yourself one person who is suffering, whether you know them or not. Pray for them if you pray. If you do not, hold them in your mind with as much goodwill as you can for a few minutes, and wish them rest, help and peace.
practices.why: Zosima asks his monks to pray each day for those who are dying, unseen, all over the earth. Even if no one knows, he says, the prayer goes out to them.
variations: Name someone you find hard to love.
Name everyone who died today, unknown.
Light the lamp again while you do it.

practices.name: The Grand Inquisitor’s question
practices.instructions: Read or recall the Grand Inquisitor’s charge: people do not want freedom but bread, miracle and authority. Think of one area of your life where you would rather be told what to do than choose. Write a few lines in the Inquisitor’s voice, then a few in your own reply.
practices.why: Ivan’s poem is one of the great arguments about freedom ever written. Dostoevsky gave the Inquisitor his strongest case and answered it only with a silent kiss.
variations: Open the Onda’s Philosophy page and read The Grand Inquisitor idea.
Discuss it with a friend over tea.
Ask where you hand your freedom to a screen.

practices.name: Five minutes left
practices.instructions: On Semyonovsky Square he believed he had five minutes to live and thought about how to spend them. Sit quietly and ask gently: if I had five minutes, whom would I speak to and what would I say? Then do one of those things today. If this question feels too heavy right now, skip it and take a walk.
practices.why: He later said that in those minutes every moment seemed an eternity of riches, and he swore never to waste a day. The exercise is about love and gratitude, not fear.
variations: Write the message you would send.
Call the person instead.
Spend the evening with them.

practices.name: Visit those who are forgotten
practices.instructions: Spend a morning or afternoon with people the world forgets: volunteer at a shelter or soup kitchen, visit a care home, sit with a lonely neighbour, write to a prisoner through a reputable letter scheme. Go as a guest, not a rescuer. Listen more than you speak.
practices.why: Four years among convicts showed him the human being in the most despised. His whole work insists that no one is beyond dignity or love.
variations: Go with a friend.
Bring tea and something to eat.
Go back a second time.

rules.why: Zosima says the one who lies to himself ends by losing all respect for himself and others. Every other rule here rests on this one.

rules.text: Love the one in front of you
rules.why: Ivan loves humanity and cannot stand his neighbour. Active love is for this person, today, by name.
In the novels the first to ask is the freest. Do not wait to be in the right before you say sorry.
Marmeladov, Sonya and the convicts of Omsk all keep their dignity in his eyes. Look for the human being behind the failure.
Each of us is responsible for all. When something goes wrong near you, ask what part is yours before you ask whose fault it is.
Keep one small place lit and cared for, a lamp, a picture, a plant, as a reminder that beauty is real.

read.title: Notes from Underground
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky
read.why: A spiteful, brilliant man in a cellar argues against reason itself. Short, savage and the key to everything after it.

read.title: Crime and Punishment
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, trans. Oliver Ready
read.why: A poor student kills an old pawnbroker to prove he is extraordinary, and his conscience hunts him through the summer streets.

read.title: The Idiot
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky
read.why: His attempt to portray a perfectly good man, Prince Myshkin, and what the world does with him.

read.title: Demons
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky
read.why: A provincial town possessed by revolutionary ideas. Prophetic, comic and terrifying.

read.title: The Brothers Karamazov
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky, trans. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky
read.why: Three brothers, their father’s murder, the Grand Inquisitor and the elder Zosima. His last and greatest novel.

read.title: White Nights
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
read.why: Four luminous Petersburg nights and a lonely dreamer in love. The gentlest door into his world.

read.title: The House of the Dead
read.creator: Fyodor Dostoevsky
read.why: A fictionalised memoir of his four years in the Omsk prison camp. Tolstoy thought it his best book.

read.title: Dostoevsky: Reminiscences
read.creator: Anna Dostoevsky, trans. Beatrice Stillman
read.why: His wife’s memoir of their fourteen years: the debts, the dictation, the gambling cured, the children and the death.

watch.title: The Idiot
watch.creator: Akira Kurosawa
watch.why: Kurosawa moves Myshkin to snowbound Hokkaido after the war. Long, strange and deeply faithful in spirit.

watch.title: White Nights
watch.creator: Luchino Visconti
watch.why: Marcello Mastroianni as the dreamer on a studio-built canal city of fog and lamplight.

watch.title: Pickpocket
watch.creator: Robert Bresson
watch.why: A Paris thief who reasons like Raskolnikov. Bresson’s spare retelling of Crime and Punishment.

watch.title: Une femme douce
watch.creator: Robert Bresson
watch.why: Bresson’s film of A Gentle Creature, the story of a husband beside the body of the wife who has killed herself. Dominique Sanda’s first role.

listen.title: All-Night Vigil
listen.creator: Sergei Rachmaninoff
listen.why: Russian Orthodox chant set for unaccompanied choir. The sound of the churches Alyosha and Zosima prayed in.

listen.title: From the House of the Dead
listen.creator: Leoš Janáček
listen.why: Janáček’s last opera, drawn from the prison memoir. Its motto: in every creature a spark of God.

listen.title: The Gambler
listen.creator: Sergei Prokofiev
listen.why: The opera of the novella he dictated in twenty-six days to escape a ruinous contract.

listen.title: Pictures at an Exhibition
listen.creator: Modest Mussorgsky
listen.why: Written in Petersburg in the years of Demons by a composer who also knew poverty and drink.

art.title: The Body of the Dead Christ in the Tomb
art.creator: Hans Holbein the Younger
art.why: In Basel in 1867 he stood on a chair before it until Anna feared a fit. A man could lose his faith from that picture, says Myshkin.

art.title: Portrait of Fyodor Dostoevsky
art.creator: Vasily Perov
art.why: Painted for Pavel Tretyakov: hands clasped round a knee, eyes inward. Anna thought it caught him in a moment of creation.

art.title: Sistine Madonna
art.creator: Raphael
art.why: His favourite painting, in Dresden. A large photograph of it hung over the sofa where he died.

art.title: Trinity
art.creator: Andrei Rublev
art.why: The great Russian icon of three angels at a table. The beauty he hoped would save the world looks like this.

art.title: Acis and Galatea
art.creator: Claude Lorrain
art.why: In Dresden. The dream of a golden age of innocence that appears in Demons and The Adolescent.

eat.title: Shchi
eat.creator: Cabbage soup
eat.why: The soup of every Russian table and of the prison camp. In The House of the Dead the convicts’ soup is shchi, thin and full of cockroaches.

eat.title: Black rye bread
eat.creator: Sour, dense and dark
eat.why: The bread of the poor and of prisoners, and in Russian piety a gift not to be wasted.

eat.title: Buckwheat kasha
eat.creator: Toasted buckwheat porridge
eat.why: The plain food of students and soldiers. Raskolnikov lives on almost nothing in his coffin of a room.

eat.title: Pirozhki
eat.creator: Small baked or fried filled buns
eat.why: Sold hot from trays in the Haymarket, where Raskolnikov wanders among the stalls.

drink.title: Strong black tea
drink.creator: From a samovar, sweetened with sugar or jam
drink.why: He drank it very strong late into the night while he wrote. Anna kept it coming.

drink.title: Kvass
drink.creator: Lightly fermented rye drink
drink.why: The everyday drink of the street. Raskolnikov’s world smells of it in the July heat.

drink.title: Kissel
drink.creator: A thick fruit drink set with starch
drink.why: A homely Russian sweet drink of berries, the kind served at a children’s table.

customs.title: Writing through the night
customs.creator: His working hours
customs.why: He wrote from late evening until dawn with tea and cigarettes, slept until late morning and dictated the night’s pages to Anna by day.

customs.title: The Gospel from Tobolsk
customs.creator: A book kept for life
customs.why: Wives of the Decembrists gave him a New Testament on his way to Siberia. He read it in prison and asked Anna to read from it as he died.

customs.title: Khristos voskrese
customs.creator: The Easter greeting
customs.why: Christ is risen; Truly he is risen; and three kisses. His story The Peasant Marey is a memory of an Easter in the camp.

customs.title: Dictation
customs.creator: How the late novels were made
customs.why: From The Gambler on, he dictated to Anna, who took it down in shorthand and wrote it out clean.

games.title: Roulette
games.creator: Game of chance
games.why: His passion and his ruin in the German spas, ended for good in Wiesbaden in 1871. Here a game for watching the pull of chance, never for money.

games.title: Durak
games.creator: Card game
games.why: The fool: the most popular card game in Russia, where the loser is the one left holding cards.

games.title: Gorodki
games.creator: Skittles game
games.why: A Russian game of throwing a bat at figures built of wooden pins. Peasants and later Tolstoy and Lenin played it.

festivals.title: Easter
festivals.creator: Russian Orthodox Easter, March to May
festivals.why: The midnight service, the bells, the greeting Christ is risen. Sonya, Lazarus and the Easter in the camp all point here.

festivals.title: Dostoevsky’s birthday
festivals.creator: 11 November (30 October in the old calendar)
festivals.why: Born in 1821 in a hospital for the poor in Moscow, where his father was a doctor.

festivals.title: The White Nights
festivals.creator: St Petersburg, late May to mid July
festivals.why: When the sun barely sets and the city stays pale all night. Walk the embankments as his dreamer did.

places.title: Dostoevsky Literary-Memorial Museum
places.creator: Kuznechny Lane, St Petersburg
places.why: The flat where he wrote The Brothers Karamazov and died in 1881. His study, his clock stopped at the hour of his death.

places.title: Sennaya Square and Stolyarny Lane
places.creator: St Petersburg
places.why: The Haymarket and its back streets, where Raskolnikov lived and walked. He counted the steps from his door.

places.title: Optina Pustyn
places.creator: Near Kozelsk, Kaluga region
places.why: The monastery he visited with Vladimir Solovyov in 1878 after his son’s death. Its elder Ambrose stands behind Zosima.

places.title: Dostoevsky House-Museum
places.creator: Staraya Russa, Novgorod region
places.why: The family’s summer house. The town became Skotoprigonyevsk in The Brothers Karamazov.

places.title: Tikhvin Cemetery
places.creator: Alexander Nevsky Lavra, St Petersburg
places.why: His grave, carved with the verse from John about the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.

ethics.title: Active love
ethics.text: Love in dreams wants quick results and applause. Active love is labour and patience, and for some people a whole science.
ethics.practice: Do one patient, unglamorous thing for someone who will not thank you.

ethics.title: Responsibility for all
ethics.text: Not guilt for everything, but refusing to stand outside: what happens around you is partly yours to answer for.
ethics.practice: When something goes wrong today, ask first what part of it is yours.

ethics.title: Humility
ethics.text: Loving humility is a terrible force, the strongest of all, says Zosima. It disarms where argument hardens.
ethics.practice: In one disagreement today, give way where it costs your pride and nothing else.

ethics.title: Honesty with oneself
ethics.text: Lies to oneself come first, and every other lie grows from them. Truth starts inside.
ethics.practice: Name one thing you have been pretending not to know.

ethics.title: Do not judge
ethics.text: The worst sinner in the novels can still be saved, and the righteous can be cruel. Judgement belongs elsewhere.
ethics.practice: Catch yourself judging someone today and imagine their story for one minute.

ethics.title: Forgiveness
ethics.text: To forgive is not to excuse but to refuse to let the wrong decide who the other person is forever.
ethics.practice: Forgive one small debt today, out loud or in your heart.

philosophy.title: The underground
philosophy.text: The underground man insists on his right to act against his own interest, just to prove he is free and not a piano key. Spite is a twisted kind of freedom.
philosophy.practice: Notice one moment today when you chose against your own good to make a point.

philosophy.title: Everything is permitted
philosophy.text: Ivan argues that without God and immortality there is no ground for virtue. Smerdyakov takes him at his word and kills. Ideas have consequences.
philosophy.practice: Ask of one idea you hold: what would someone do who believed it completely?

philosophy.title: The Grand Inquisitor
philosophy.text: The Inquisitor says people do not want freedom but bread, miracle and authority, and he loves them by taking their freedom away. Christ answers with a kiss.
philosophy.practice: Where today would you rather be told what to do than choose? Choose.

philosophy.title: Suffering and its meaning
philosophy.text: His characters are changed by suffering, but he also shows suffering that only crushes. The question is what love can do with it, not whether to seek it.
philosophy.practice: Think of one hard time that changed you. What helped it become something other than damage?

philosophy.title: Polyphony
philosophy.text: Bakhtin saw that his characters argue with full voices that the author does not silence. Truth emerges between people, in dialogue.
philosophy.practice: Let the strongest version of a view you oppose speak in your head for five minutes.

philosophy.title: Beauty will save the world
philosophy.text: Beauty here is not prettiness but the radiance of the good, glimpsed in a face, an icon or a child. It can draw people where argument cannot.
philosophy.practice: Find one beautiful thing today and stay with it for a full minute.

philosophy.title: The double
philosophy.text: We split ourselves to escape what we are, and the split comes back as a double that shames us. Wholeness is the cure.
philosophy.practice: Where are you one person in public and another alone? Name the gap.

philosophy.title: The holy fool
philosophy.text: Myshkin is defenceless, honest and kind, and he exposes everyone around him without meaning to. Goodness looks like foolishness to the world.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today that is simply good and looks a little foolish.

journal: Where did I lie to myself today?
Who was the person in front of me today, and did I love them actively?
What did I resent today, and what was underneath it?
What part of something that went wrong today was mine?
Whom do I need to ask for forgiveness, and what stops me?
When did my pride make me act against my own good?
What beauty did I see today?
Which idea of mine would be dangerous if someone acted on it fully?
Where am I a dreamer, living in fantasy rather than in my days?
Who have I judged, and what might their story be?
What would I do with five more minutes of life, and why am I not doing it?
What is my underground: the cellar where my spite lives?
When did I want bread, miracle or authority instead of freedom?
Which voice in me have I been silencing?
What humbles me, and what does humility make possible?
Who in my life is a holy fool, honest past the point of sense?
What do I owe to people I have never met?
When did suffering change me, and what made the difference?
Where in my life is there a double, a second self I do not admit?
What gamble am I tempted by, with money, time or love?
What did a child teach me recently?
What does my conscience keep returning to?
Where did I love humanity today and fail a human being?
What would Zosima say to me tonight?
What would Ivan say, and how would I answer him?
What did I see today that I would rather not have seen?
Whom have I written off, and could I be wrong?
What is the corner of my life I keep lit?
What would I like to be resurrected in me?
What has this Onda shown me about my soul?
reflect: What have you learned about lying to yourself?
What did active love ask of you, and did you give it?
Which character did you most recognise yourself in?
What did you come to see about responsibility for others?
Where did you find beauty, and did it change anything?
What will you carry from Dostoevsky into ordinary days?
dayThemes: The person in front of you

intro: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow in 1821, the son of a doctor at a hospital for the poor. He trained as a military engineer in St Petersburg, resigned to write, and became famous overnight in 1846 when the critic Belinsky hailed his first novel, Poor Folk.

In 1849 he was arrested with a circle of young men who met to read banned socialist writings. They were sentenced to death, tied to posts on Semyonovsky Square and reprieved at the last moment by a message from the Tsar that had been planned all along. He spent four years at hard labour in Omsk and five more as a soldier in Siberia.

Prison changed him. Among murderers and thieves he found faith in the Russian people, in Christ and in the dignity of the most degraded human being. He came back to Petersburg in 1859 with a New Testament he had carried through the camp and a hatred of tidy theories that promise happiness by calculation.

The great novels followed in a rush, written against deadlines, debts, epilepsy and a gambling passion that ruined him in the German spas until he gave it up in 1871: Notes from Underground, Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and finally The Brothers Karamazov. His second wife, Anna, a stenographer, took them down from dictation and made their life possible.

His books are arguments with many voices. Atheists, saints, murderers, holy fools and drunkards each speak with full force, and he lets them. What he believed comes through his elders and fools: that we must not lie to ourselves, that love is a labour done for real people, that each of us is responsible for all, and that freedom is both our dignity and our torment.

This Onda takes from him a way of living, not a creed: honesty with oneself, active love for the person in front of you, the courage to ask forgiveness first, attention to beauty, and a refusal to give up on anyone. It also invites you into his Petersburg of white nights, icon lamps and strong tea.
guide.origin: Moscow, St Petersburg, Siberia, and years abroad in Dresden, Geneva and Florence
guide.era: Dostoevsky was born in 1821 and died in St Petersburg in 1881, months after The Brothers Karamazov was finished

figures.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
figures.bio: Novelist, journalist and former convict. Short, pale and intense, a brilliant reader aloud and a ruinous gambler until he stopped.

figures.name: Anna Grigoryevna Dostoevskaya
figures.bio: The stenographer who took down The Gambler in 1866 and married him the next year. She managed his debts, published his books and kept his memory.

figures.name: Mikhail Dostoevsky
figures.bio: His elder brother and closest friend, with whom he ran the journals Vremya and Epokha. His death left Fyodor with his debts and family.

figures.name: Maria Dmitrievna Isaeva
figures.bio: His first wife, met in Siberia, proud and consumptive. Something of her is in Katerina Ivanovna of Crime and Punishment.

figures.name: Apollinaria Suslova
figures.bio: The young writer he loved in the 1860s and travelled with in Europe. Polina of The Gambler is drawn from her.

figures.name: Vissarion Belinsky
figures.bio: The most powerful critic of his day, who hailed Poor Folk and then fell out with its author over faith and art.

figures.name: Mikhail Petrashevsky
figures.bio: Host of the Friday gatherings where Dostoevsky read banned texts, the cause of his arrest in 1849.

figures.name: Vladimir Solovyov
figures.bio: The young religious philosopher who went with him to Optina Pustyn in 1878. Some see him in Alyosha Karamazov.

figures.name: Ambrose of Optina
figures.bio: The elder of Optina Pustyn whom Dostoevsky visited after his son’s death, a model for Zosima.

figures.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
figures.bio: The critic whose Problems of Dostoevsky’s Poetics described his novels as polyphonic, a chorus of free voices.

history.detail: In the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, where his father worked as a doctor. The date is 30 October in the old calendar.
He enters the Main Engineering School in St Petersburg. His mother has died; his father dies the next year, possibly killed by his own serfs.
His first novel, a story in letters, appears to acclaim. Belinsky calls him a new Gogol. The Double follows and is less loved.
Arrested with members of the Petrashevsky circle for reading and circulating banned writings, including Belinsky’s letter to Gogol.
On Semyonovsky Square the prisoners are prepared for shooting, then told their sentence has been commuted. It was staged.
Four years in shackles in a Siberian prison fort, the source of The House of the Dead.
Service as a private and then an officer at Semipalatinsk. In 1857 he marries Maria Isaeva.

history.what: Notes from Underground and two deaths
history.detail: His wife and his brother Mikhail die within months. He publishes the confession of the underground man.

history.what: Crime and Punishment and The Gambler
history.detail: The great novel runs in The Russian Messenger. To meet a contract he dictates The Gambler to Anna Snitkina in under a month.
Married to Anna, he flees creditors to Dresden, Geneva and Florence, writes The Idiot and begins Demons. In April 1871 he gambles for the last time.
He starts a monthly diary of essays, sketches and stories that makes him a public voice, for good and ill.
His three-year-old son dies. He visits the elders of Optina Pustyn with Solovyov and begins The Brothers Karamazov.
At the unveiling of Pushkin’s statue in Moscow he speaks of the Russian soul’s universal sympathy. The hall erupts.
His last novel is completed in November, the Grand Inquisitor and Zosima at its heart.
He dies after a haemorrhage. Tens of thousands follow his coffin to the Alexander Nevsky Lavra.

concepts.detail: Zosima tells a lady who loves humanity in dreams but cannot bear real people that active love is harsh and dreadful compared with love in dreams, and that it alone convinces.
Markel and Zosima teach that each of us is guilty before all for all. It is not a counsel of guilt but of joy: once you accept it, says Zosima, the world becomes paradise.
The narrator of Notes from Underground argues that people will act against their own advantage to prove they are not keys on a piano. Reason alone cannot build a happy humanity.
Ivan’s poem imagines Christ returning to Seville and arrested by a cardinal who has corrected his work, giving people bread, mystery and authority instead of a freedom too heavy for them.
Ivan’s formula, if there is no immortality, and Raskolnikov’s theory of extraordinary men show reasoning that ends in blood. Dostoevsky tests ideas by living them out.
Bakhtin argued that in these novels the characters are not mouthpieces but independent consciousnesses, and that the novel’s truth lies in their dialogue.
Following the Russian tradition of the yurodivy, Myshkin and others are mocked as simple yet see and say what others hide.
With his brother he called on educated Russians to reconnect with the faith and life of the common people, against both Westernisers and Slavophiles.
Beauty is mysterious and terrible, says Dmitri Karamazov: there God and the devil are fighting, and the battlefield is the human heart. Myshkin hopes it will save the world.

facts.text: He was led out to be shot in 1849 and reprieved at the last minute. He later said he had perhaps five minutes left and thought about how to spend them.
He suffered from epilepsy and gave his attacks, with their moment of ecstatic clarity, to Prince Myshkin.
He dictated The Gambler in twenty-six days in 1866 to meet a contract that would otherwise have given a publisher his work for free for nine years.
Anna Dostoevskaya invented a shorthand-based system for keeping his accounts and became one of Russia’s first women publishers by selling his books herself.
He gave up gambling in 1871 after a final loss in Wiesbaden and never returned to it.
The Brothers Karamazov’s monastery and elder draw on his visit to Optina Pustyn in 1878.
Freud, Einstein, Kafka, Camus and Nietzsche all read him closely. Nietzsche called him the only psychologist from whom he had anything to learn.
His grave carries John 12:24, about the grain of wheat that must fall into the earth and die, the epigraph of The Brothers Karamazov.

glossary.meaning: Siberian penal servitude with hard labour
An elder, a monk who guides others
The return to the native soil
An oil lamp kept burning before an icon

sensitivity.note: Dostoevsky’s novels are among the most humane ever written, but his journalism, above all A Writer’s Diary, also contains antisemitic passages and a fervent Russian nationalism. This Onda takes his practice of honesty, active love and responsibility. It does not take up his politics, and it never asks you to seek suffering.
requiredCaveats: A Writer’s Diary and some letters contain antisemitic statements that should be named, not excused.
His view that suffering can purify is a theme in the novels, not advice. Suffering is not to be sought, and no one should be told to endure abuse.
His religious faith was Russian Orthodox; the practices here are open to readers of any faith or none.

immersePlan.name: Read White Nights in one evening
immersePlan.text: His gentlest story: four nights, a dreamer and a girl on a Petersburg embankment. Read it in one sitting, ideally by a window at dusk.

immersePlan.name: Read Part One of the underground
immersePlan.text: Read the first part of Notes from Underground, the monologue. Mark every place where you recognise yourself, however unwillingly.

immersePlan.name: Read the Grand Inquisitor
immersePlan.text: Read Book 5, chapters 4 and 5 of The Brothers Karamazov: Rebellion and The Grand Inquisitor. Then sit for a while with Christ’s silent answer.

immersePlan.name: Watch Bresson’s Pickpocket
immersePlan.text: Watch Robert Bresson’s spare Paris retelling of Crime and Punishment. Notice how little is said, and how much the hands reveal.

immersePlan.name: Watch Visconti’s White Nights
immersePlan.text: Watch Marcello Mastroianni as the dreamer in Visconti’s foggy canal city, then compare it with the story you read.

immersePlan.name: Watch Kurosawa’s Idiot
immersePlan.text: Watch Kurosawa’s snowbound Hokkaido version of The Idiot. Watch how goodness unsettles everyone around it.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the All-Night Vigil
immersePlan.text: Listen to Rachmaninoff’s All-Night Vigil in a darkened room. It is the sound of the Orthodox churches his characters pray in.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Janáček’s prison opera
immersePlan.text: Listen to the overture and first act of From the House of the Dead, drawn from his years in Omsk. Read its motto first: in every creature a spark of God.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Prokofiev’s Gambler
immersePlan.text: Listen to the roulette scene of Prokofiev’s opera The Gambler, from the novella Dostoevsky dictated in twenty-six days.

immersePlan.name: Stand before Holbein’s dead Christ
immersePlan.text: Look at Holbein’s Dead Christ for five minutes, as he did in Basel. Ask what Myshkin meant: a man could lose his faith from that picture.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Sistine Madonna
immersePlan.text: Look at Raphael’s Sistine Madonna, his favourite painting, which hung above the sofa where he died. Look at the mother’s eyes and the child’s.

immersePlan.name: Contemplate Rublev’s Trinity
immersePlan.text: Spend ten minutes with Rublev’s Trinity icon. Follow the circle of the three figures and the open place at the table.

immersePlan.name: Cook a pot of shchi
immersePlan.text: Cook shchi, the cabbage soup of every Russian table and of the prison camp. Eat it with black bread and think of who ate it with you.

immersePlan.name: Eat a student’s kasha
immersePlan.text: Make buckwheat kasha with a little butter, the plain food of poor students like Raskolnikov. Eat it slowly and gratefully.

immersePlan.name: Bake or buy pirozhki
immersePlan.text: Bake or buy pirozhki, the filled buns sold hot in the Haymarket, and share them with someone.

immersePlan.name: Drink tea the night-writer’s way
immersePlan.text: Brew strong black tea and drink it from a glass in a holder, with a spoon of jam, while you read or write in the evening.

immersePlan.name: Taste kvass
immersePlan.text: Find or make kvass, the lightly fermented rye drink of Russian streets. Taste its sourness and think of a hot Petersburg July.

immersePlan.name: Make berry kissel
immersePlan.text: Make kissel, the thick berry drink set with starch, and serve it warm or cold to someone you love.

immersePlan.name: Keep one night writer’s evening
immersePlan.text: Keep his hours for one evening: tea at ten, writing or reading until past midnight, the house dark around you. Sleep in if you can.

immersePlan.name: Learn the Easter greeting
immersePlan.text: Learn the Easter greeting, Khristos voskrese, and the answer, Voistinu voskrese. Read his short story The Peasant Marey.

immersePlan.name: Dictate a page to a friend
immersePlan.text: Dictate a page of a letter or story to a friend while they write it down, as he dictated his novels to Anna. Notice how speaking changes your words.

immersePlan.name: Play a game of durak
immersePlan.text: Learn and play durak, the most popular card game in Russia, where the loser is the fool left holding cards.

immersePlan.name: Try gorodki
immersePlan.text: Set up a simple game of gorodki with sticks or skittles in a park, throwing a bat to knock the figures out of the square.

immersePlan.name: Watch the pull of chance
immersePlan.text: Watch a roulette wheel online or spin a coin twenty times without any money involved, and notice the urge to predict and to win. That pull ruined him.

immersePlan.name: Go to a midnight Easter service
immersePlan.text: If you can, attend an Orthodox Easter vigil at midnight, or watch one, and hear the greeting Christ is risen pass from mouth to mouth.

immersePlan.name: Visit his last flat
immersePlan.text: Visit, or explore online, his last flat on Kuznechny Lane, where he wrote The Brothers Karamazov and died.

immersePlan.name: Walk Raskolnikov’s route
immersePlan.text: Walk, or follow on a map, the route from Raskolnikov’s house to the pawnbroker’s: about seven hundred and thirty steps, he wrote.

immersePlan.name: Learn the word dusha
immersePlan.text: Learn dusha, soul, and the phrase po dushe, heart to heart. Use it in your thoughts each time you speak sincerely today.

immersePlan.name: Learn the word toska
immersePlan.text: Learn toska, the aching longing with no clear object. Notice when you feel it today and give it its name.

immersePlan.name: Learn the words for active love
immersePlan.text: Learn deyatelnaya lyubov, active love, and write down one act of it you will do this week.
